interest: This collection provides a compelling window into the wartime transformation of international intellectual property from a private commercial concern into an instrument of economic warfare. In 1940, the State and Commerce Departments handled an alleged patent infringement through normal bilateral legal channels, advising an American inventor to retain local Japanese counsel. By early 1943, following the outbreak of the Pacific War, the documents illustrate how the Japanese Board of Technology and Patent Office methodically cancelled enemy patent protections and issued an Imperial decree to seize and exploit vital American industrial technologies—including DuPont's synthetic rubber, Westinghouse's electric welding, and General Electric's light bulbs. Additionally, the file reveals the multi-agency intelligence efforts of the U.S. government, showing how the State Department, the FCC (via broadcast intercepts), and the FBI (via intercepted Axis communications between Japan and Germany) tracked Japan's technical utilization of Allied patents while the U.S. Alien Property Custodian enacted reciprocal policies at home.
overview: This file (State Department decimal file 894.542, Intellectual and Industrial Property: Patents) consists of correspondence, internal memoranda, and intelligence reports from June 1940 and February–March 1943 regarding foreign patent rights in Japan and the treatment of enemy patents during World War II. The pre-war material addresses a private patent infringement dispute involving an American hooked rug machine in Japan, handled through commercial and consular legal channels. The wartime documentation from 1943 tracks the Japanese Imperial government's systematic cancellation and industrial exploitation of approximately 3,000 enemy-owned patents (roughly half of which were American, including critical manufacturing processes of DuPont, General Electric, and Westinghouse). These wartime developments were compiled by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs using Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service/FCC intercepts and an FBI report on diplomatic transmissions between Japan and Germany, alongside an internal State Department memorandum confirming that the U.S. Alien Property Custodian had reciprocally seized Japanese patents for domestic use.

subfiles.about: Report on the administrative disposition of an alleged patent infringement case in Japan involving an American hooked rug machine.
subfiles.from: George Wythe and James L. Brown
subfiles.summary: Liaison Officer George Wythe and Acting Chief James L. Brown of the Department of Commerce write to Raymond H. Geist of the Department of State regarding an alleged patent infringement in Japan of a hooked rug machine owned by Albert White of New York. Following consultation between the Commerce Department's New York District Office and White's attorney, Samuel H. Feinson, Feinson agreed to engage a correspondent attorney in Tokyo from an official consular list. The Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce notes that it has closed its file on the case and asks that the American Consulate and Assistant Commercial Attaché in Tokyo be informed.
subfiles.title: Letter from George Wythe and James L. Brown to Raymond H. Geist regarding patent infringement of hooked rug machine

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Japanese cancellation and industrial utilization of enemy-owned patents during World War II.
subfiles.summary: Foreign Service Officer Frank S. Williams reports to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Japanese wartime policy regarding roughly 3,000 enemy-owned patents, half of which belonged to U.S. entities. Citing an article in the Japan Times and Advertiser and FCC radio intercepts, Williams notes that the Japanese Board of Technology had cancelled 1,087 enemy patents by December 1942, while an Imperial order directed their aggressive utilization. He concludes that Japanese industry was actively using prominent American patents, including DuPont's synthetic rubber, General Electric's light bulbs, and Westinghouse's electric welding processes.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by Frank S. Williams on Japanese cancellation and utilization of enemy patents

subfiles.about: Brief internal memorandum confirming that the U.S. Alien Property Custodian had seized enemy patents for American domestic use.
subfiles.summary: H. Merrell Benninghoff of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs records a response regarding American handling of Japanese patents. In consultation with Mr. Ward of the Office of the Legal Adviser, Benninghoff states that the Alien Property Custodian had taken custody of all enemy patents and was making them available for use by domestic American manufacturing firms.
subfiles.title: Memorandum by H. Merrell Benninghoff on U.S. treatment of Japanese patents

subfiles.about: Duplicate official copy with routing initials of Frank S. Williams's memorandum on Japanese exploitation of Allied patents.
subfiles.summary: This document is an official duplicate copy, bearing division routing initials, of Frank S. Williams's February 24, 1943 memorandum to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It outlines the cancellation of over 1,000 enemy patents by the Japanese Board of Technology and the Japanese government's Imperial order facilitating the utilization of hostile patent rights. It highlights the strategic adoption by Japan of major American industrial techniques, including DuPont synthetic rubber, Westinghouse electric welding, General Electric incandescent lamps, and Gillette safety razors.
subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum by Frank S. Williams on Japanese cancellation and utilization of enemy patents

subfiles.about: FBI memorandum conveying intelligence on an intercepted transmission from Japan to Germany regarding the revocation of enemy patents.
subfiles.summary: FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover provides confidential intelligence to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. concerning enemy patents registered in Japan. Based on a confidential source, Hoover reports that a January 2, 1943 message from Japan to Germany noted that out of 3,000 enemy patents registered at the war's outset, more than 1,000 had been revoked, several hundred had expired, and the remainder were slated for imminent cancellation.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from J. Edgar Hoover to Adolf A. Berle, Jr. regarding enemy patents registered in Japan
